utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-03-69-T. The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Let's first check whether the videolink is functioning well. Mr. Bogunovic, can you hear me and can you see me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you. And, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Mr. Jordash, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. And before we start, Mr. Bogunovic, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I ask for P553 to be on e-court, please. And page 9 of the English and page 10 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, would you look at paragraph 52, please, which states: "We found out about Ovcara much later. It was rarely mentioned because the people who were there were not allowed to talk about it and were afraid. It was Vujovic and Vujanovic who forbid any discussion about this. Since they were commanders, I'm convinced that it was them who forbid any discussion, and if it wasn't for them, then Ovcara wouldn't have happened." Have you reminded yourself of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just in two or three sentences, could you explain what happened, as you understood it, at Ovcara in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand, some of the prisoners stayed behind in Vukovar, or rather, in Velepromet. At that time the commanders were Vujovic and Vujanovic, and instead of taking people to Serbia, those people were taken to Ovcara and were executed there. We didn't know about that immediately after the event. A lot of time lapsed until the story became public and until we all found out what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And Vujovic is Miroljub Vujovic; is that right? M-i-r-o-l-j-u-b.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was he tried for this crime?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where was he tried?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade, at the special court there in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And he received, is this right, a 40-year sentence?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so or perhaps 20. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And am I correct that Vujovic was known at the time or became known soon after as somebody who -- just give me a moment, please. Did Vujovic have a particular reputation at the time of these events as somebody who was not willing to respect the laws of war and respect civilians?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't know Vujovic. I did not know him from before. He was not a member of my party. He was not a party member. I knew very little about him, but I did know the men who preceded him as commanders and that's why I said without knowing them that maybe it wasn't a good thing to have them appointed to those positions. I don't know whether he had the reputation that you described, however, whatever you just said turned out to be the truth after those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have P407 on e-court, please. Not to be broadcast. Thank you. Could we go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, I don't know if you recall this from yesterday, but it is or purports to be a state security report from Novi Sad to Jovica Stanisic. Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's go to page 1 then, please. Let's just make sure we both understand what we are looking at. Do you see the first page, Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Chief of the state security department?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the subject is a report, one copy of the report on Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we go over the page to page 2, and the first paragraph there, just have a look and remind yourself of this which we looked at yesterday.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The first paragraph describes what appears to be some kind of staged or fake clash between Kojic and Vujovic, the same Vujovic we were speaking about in relation to Ovcara. Yesterday when you were asked about it by my learned friend for the Prosecution - Your Honours page 25 of the draft transcript - you described something a little different, which was a genuine argument between Kojic and Vujovic. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you agree with me that this report from your experience is inaccurate and that the disagreement between Kojic and Vujovic was, in fact, quite genuine?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure it was genuine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And do you know the basis of the disagreement between the two?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis of the disagreement aligned the fact that Vujovic did what he wanted. He did things that he was not authorised to do, that he was not supposed to do. When he was called to task and when he was told that he should not go on doing them, he opposed and he said that he would blow up the police building if need be just to prevent things from being the way they wanted them to be. In other words, the argument was genuine and I'm sure that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So is this accurate then: Vujovic was a threat to the work of the police as Ilija Kojic saw it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And not just a threat to the police, but a threat to the security of ordinary civilians in the region?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I must say that the TO was joined by people whom we didn't know. There were robberies, murders, and the security situation was rather bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So returning to the Exhibit P407 and the second paragraph: "The source said Serbia was to blame for all these developments, that is, the assistant minister of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, Jovica Stanisic, who tried to use Ivkovic, Kojic, Kostic, and others to turn the Krajina into a 'twilight zone.'" Would you agree with this that Kojic was, in fact, certainly in the context of Vujovic, trying to prevent Vujovic from causing chaos in the region?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. Not only did Kojic want that, but also people from the government, or rather, the residents of the area did not feel safe. They feared Vujovic's men and what they were doing and how they behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Looking at -- thank you, Mr. Bogunovic. Looking at paragraph 3: "Visic also accused Kojic of obstructing the work of the SUP, preventing inspection service, the police and municipal organs from working, and all this was covered up by shady deals involving the export of wood (oak) from the Krajina, oil, and other alleged shady deals." Did you experience Kojic trying to obstruct the work of the SUP as described in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kojic cannot obstruct that because Kojic was not the only one working in the police. There were others around him, and it is certain that the police, including Kojic, tried to prevent things that were happening at the time. In addition to the selling of oaks there were the instances of theft from the companies that were closed down at that time and also things were being stolen from private individuals, including tractors and other agricultural equipment. I can't say that he was the one who tried to obstruct things. It was the police that did their job, that tried to uphold the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we turn now, please, to P554. Could we go to page 5 of the English version and 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the paragraph I'm interested in, Mr. Bogunovic, is paragraph 24. If you just read that to yourself quickly to remind yourself of it.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The sentence I'm particularly interested in or the two sentences are those at the end: "After the fall of Vukovar, I requested reinforce for the police force and in fact 300 police officers arrived from Serbia in Vukovar to control the situation because the JNA had left. I tried to restore some order and legality and control from the authority." Could you explain or elaborate on that, please.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the JNA left Vukovar killings started. People were being killed irrespective of their ethnicity or religion. It didn't matter whether they were Serbs, Croats, Hungarians. If they had property, be it a good vehicle or some money, they would be killed. There were robberies, murders of civilians and residents of the area. Things were being transported across the border to Serbia. At one point I asked for reinforcement for the police to come over from Serbia in order to help us restore order and prevent further murders and robberies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Who did you request those reinforcements from?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a meeting. I don't remember when. Goran was with me. We had a meeting. I believe that it was in Belgrade. I'm not sure. No, I'm sure it was in Belgrade. But I don't know who we met with. I asked those people to help us overcome the situation and restore order.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And when the 300 police officers arrived, whose command did they fall under?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They fell under the command of the men who were in charge of the police in Slavonia and Baranja. They placed themselves at our service when they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were they of any assistance in overcoming the situation and restoring order?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. First of all, they established order on the borders. Whenever somebody wanted to transport something across the border, they had to prove the origin of those goods. Also, they established check-points in the villages and in Vukovar and they checked passengers and vehicles and they were of a major assistance in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were their duties restricted to police officer duties, I mean, traditional police officer duties of detecting and preventing crime?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of an organisation called the Serbian National Security formed under Goran Hadzic's control?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of that but that organisation was under the personal control of Goran Hadzic. Whatever they had to say, they said to him and I was not in the loop.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. This had, from what you observed, nothing to do with any other member of the SBWS government, this was Goran Hadzic's organisation?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was it disbanded by Badza after Badza arrived in the region?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I think that it continued working, and I think that those men were still under the control of Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we turn to P553, please. And page 15 of the English and 16 of the B/C/S. Sorry, 17 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 88. Do you have paragraph 88, Mr. Bogunovic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 88 describes Arkan and particular -- a particular crime committed concerning shooting people, men dead in a brickyard. And the statement describes that Arkan committed it, or you were told that he committed this crime in retaliation for the killing of several of his men in Ernestinovo in early October. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was it widely known that or did it become widely known that Arkan had committed this crime for personal reasons?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that I had heard about Arkan who had had a skirmish the day before Ernestinovo with the HVO. He had lost three men. On the following day he returned to Dalj, and he learned that there were some 15 men in the brickyard, they had been brought over from Beli Manastir. He ordered the men to be taken out of the furnaces and shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, did you hear about Arkan removing prisoners from the Dalj prison and executing them around this time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was this --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, go ahead, I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion he took a couple of people from the prison in Dalj. They were taken away and they were shot dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you speak to other members of the SBWS government about this crime?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only about that crime. The government discussed the situation. We knew that the situation was not that good. We didn't dare talk about Arkan that much because he was in the area, and we all feared him and his men. So we didn't discuss him much. Not a lot was actually said about that incident as a result of that. When we talked about Arkan and those incidents, we talked in private.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was it privately condemned by you and other members of the SBWS government?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did not like his conduct, we did not like what he did, but we were powerless to oppose him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we turn now, please, to paragraph 26 of this statement. Page 6 of the English and 6 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: "I met Jovica Stanisic several times. I had no personal contact with him. He never told me anything about what his role was." Is it right that you did not during these events speak to Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall speaking with him. I don't recall any conversations with him. I don't think there were any.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And he never told you anything about what his role was, and is it correct that no one else told you what his role was either?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some point in time, Goran told me that Jovica was from the state security but nothing other than that. He didn't specify whether he was a chief. He just said that he was from the DB and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And from that you understood what?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we met other people at the time as well. We wanted to meet anyone who could assist us, provide advice or instructions about what to do. We wanted to meet people who could provide us with what we needed the most at the time, be it financially or in other ways. In any case, that was the reason why we met with people from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But you knew Stanisic -- let me start that again. Hadzic told you Stanisic was from the DB, but through these events, as you told us yesterday, you had no idea what role the DB played, if any, in the SBWS in 1991 and 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Looking at this paragraph again, the paragraph says: "If he had to talk to anyone, he spoke to Goran Hadzic. I met him in Backa Palanka and in Novi Sad. I went to these places to meet Goran Hadzic but those were not official meetings with Stanisic, he just happened to be there." Now, how do you know that if Stanisic had to talk to anyone he spoke to Goran Hadzic? Did that come from Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So Goran Hadzic mentioned to you that, for example, he had gone to Belgrade and met with Stanisic, is that what he was saying at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that only to me, he shared it the other members of the government as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But from what you told us at no time did Hadzic inform you what Stanisic had said or what Stanisic had instructed or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't specify any instructions. He only said that he had met with Stanisic and that they had spoken. He would then convey specific instructions about how to go about solving our problems the way that would be favourable for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But wasn't Hadzic saying that those instructions were coming from Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, for the most part he would say he had been to see Milosevic and that he had arranged with him what needs to be done and what would be the best course to take for us. It happened frequently that he said he had seen Milosevic and received instructions from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just take instructions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry for the delay, Mr. Bogunovic. Just to pick up where we left off, is it right -- well, let me ask you it in a more open way. Can you recall any instruction whatsoever from either Stanisic or anyone from the Serbian DB in relation to your work within the SBWS?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall any instructions from Stanisic since I didn't know who the man was. I was introduced to him by Badza with whom I had more frequent contacts, but before meeting him in Backa Palanka and Novi Sad, I had not met him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just so that you understand our position, Mr. Bogunovic, Mr. Stanisic has no recollection of meeting you in Backa Palanka. Are you sure that your recollection is correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall having met him at Ljubo Novakovic's place in Backa Palanka. I don't know how long the meeting lasted, but I do recall that particular encounter. I remember him being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. But in any event, whoever's recollection is correct, from what you recall, Stanisic didn't say anything but simply sat and took notes?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember him saying anything. There were several of us there and the municipal president of Backa Palanka spoke the most, as well as some people from Novi Sad, but I didn't hear Jovica Stanisic utter a single word.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The meeting that you recall was focused on and concerned with the plight of refugees in the Backa Palanka region; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's correct, isn't it, that you never saw Stanisic in the SBWS region in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you never heard that he had attended a meeting in November of 1991 involving members of the SBWS government?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you were never told that Stanisic attended prior to the fall of Vukovar and screamed and shouted at members of the SBWS government berating them for failing to take Vukovar? You never heard about that; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm almost finished, Mr. Bogunovic. I just wanted to ask you about something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Please could we go to P554. Page 4 of the English and 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Paragraph 18, Mr. Bogunovic. "My impression is that Hadzic was controlled by the authorities in Belgrade. As well I was appointed as minister of the interior but the decisions regarding my police force were taken also in Belgrade by others." Am I correct that -- no, let me strike that. What do you mean by that? Was this just an impression you gained that Hadzic was influenced by authorities in Belgrade? Is that a more accurate way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't only my impression. Goran Hadzic, as I've said, frequently went to Belgrade. He often went to see Milosevic and upon his return he would tell us, this is no good, we should go about it differently, and he would say that we were to keep in mind that we would be called to task about what we are doing because he had to go to Belgrade and explain to them what is going on. I gathered from that that what I stated in the statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. Would you agree that rather than Hadzic being controlled, he was influenced by authorities in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, this question has now been put twice to the witness and the answer is different than the first time he says no, the way in which I said it in my statement is right. And the second time you ask him he comes to a different conclusion. So I'd rather explore that. Mr. Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash makes a distinction between being influenced and being controlled. Now, the difference apparently is that when Mr. Hadzic came back from Belgrade, did he tell you that he listened to Belgrade and made up his mind himself, whether or not following what was suggested to him, or did he give you the impression that he was expected to follow any proposals or suggestions and that he was not expected to do it in any way different from what was suggested or proposed to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that both was the case. Sometimes he would say plainly, we have to do this, and that he was requested to do so. However, there were other cases when he said it would be wise to do it because it is believed that it will be good for us. So both instances took place. There were orders and the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean, have I understood you well, that you gained the impression that Mr. Hadzic was not always free to act in accordance with his own views if they were different from Belgrade and that sometimes he was not free to choose his own options but had to follow what was the preference of Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he had to do what was expected of him and what he was ordered to do in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did it depend on the subject whether you gained the impression that he could follow his own views or whether he was expected to do what was proposed or suggested to him? Did it make any difference on what kind of subjects they had been talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my impression that the issue in question was important. It depended on what needed to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you give us examples of issues where you thought that he was free to take a different route as suggested by Belgrade, and an example of another subject where he felt that he was not free to choose his own preferred route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can tell you this: There were cases when Goran returned from Belgrade and said that what we had done thus far and the way we followed can no longer be, and that things needed to change. We were expected to follow what we had been told. To us it was a sign that we had to accept it, but there were also situations in which he said that things were proposed to him but that we would continue along our designated line. Sometimes we accepted that and frequently we had no other choice. We were dependent on Belgrade's and Serbia's assistance, hence, we had no room to make our own decision or to reject anything. My removal from the ministerial position was on the proposal of Radovan Stojicic, Badza. At first my colleagues refused to have me removed but at the next government session, Goran called me aside and he said, it's better that you left. We need to do this because it is requested of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From whom -- by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was requested or the way Badza said was that there was an order for him to ask for my removal. It came from Belgrade. Goran had been summoned there whereupon he was told that I needed to be removed. I don't know whether he went to see Milosevic or someone else, but that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have, please, P2669. 65 ter, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't aware that we were already in that number as far as P exhibits are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Page 1, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, would you just have a look at this which appears to be minutes from a session of the government of SBWS held on the 28th of November, 1991, in Erdut. I'd like you to, if you would, just take a few moments to read it through. Please indicate when you've finished the particular page.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm done with the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Go to the second page then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm done with the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Go to 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm done reading the third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let's leave it there. That's probably enough for my purposes. Do you recall this session?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was this type of decision-making as reflected in these minutes typical of a government meeting of that time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we go back to page 1, the Ilija Kojic is missing from this session. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was there a reason for that, do you know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was wounded and that he was hopitalised in Belgrade at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the agenda 2 was -- is report and crime in the Serbian district and proposed measures to counter it. Is it correct that the government, the SBWS were making the principal decisions about how to deal with crime in the SBWS region?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could I ask you to clarify the question about type of decision-making. I've got no idea, apparently the witness has, but I've got no idea what type, is it that you follow an agenda, is it that you give a brief explanation of the decision-making in the minutes, but what is the type of decision-making you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I was coming to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness has already said yes. I have no idea how to understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I was hoping to elaborate on that with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you think the witness would have understood -- we could ask the witness. Mr. Bogunovic, Mr. Jordash asked you whether this was, this type of decision-making, was that typical of a government meeting. Could you tell us how you understood that question? What type of decision-making Mr. Jordash, as you understood him, was referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Jordash please switch off his mike when he is not using it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had in mind the decisions based on the information that was presented at that meeting. The information was provided by people who lived in the area and who either came to me or to Hadzic to convey that information to us. We in our turn presented that information at government sessions. It was already close to the end of the war and the individuals who were there and who committed thefts or any other criminal acts, their doings were put on the agenda, we discussed that point on the agenda, and we made decisions based on our discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what you had in your mind, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whether that's the type of decision-making is still unclear to me but, okay, at least we now understand what was on your mind. If you want to further explore the matter, please feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And item 2 there, please have a look at that: "In addition to the written report, he sent Milorad Trosic, district public Prosecutor, emphasised that after the liberation of Borovo, Naselje, and Vukovar, problems had become even more pressing and that the situation was deteriorating. There is a high incidence of speculation, tax evasions and other crimes which is having a serious effect." And then item 2 reports that these subjects were discussed amongst various people including yourself and Radovan Stojicic. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So is this correct what you were saying a moment ago is that information concerning crimes in villages and towns would be given to the government in written reports; is that correct so far?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The government including Stojicic and yourself would then discuss these issues and then decisions would be made on how to deal with the situation of crimes on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection just in the context of this report. It very clearly states with respect to this specific item in the last line of item 2 regarding the decisions. I believe we are talking about something general versus specific document. If the questions could accurately reflect what the specific document from the witness states.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'm extrapolating from the document and asking the witness to discuss generally how decisions were made. I'm not sure what Mr. Weber is suggesting I should do other than stick to the document, which I'm not prepared to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just for the record, the document last line, item 2 says, "no particular decisions were adopted."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a bit of a problem is, Mr. Jordash, that's of course is puzzling me, I see this document now for the first time that of course some of the matters apparently discussed are not decided at all, whereas others are decided in that someone will form an opinion about it. So to extrapolate from this document seems not to be easy because it covers quite different subjects. The level of decision-making is quite different as well. So if you want to extrapolate from this document, if you want to be clear, it should be fully transparent what you are extrapolating and clearly then put that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is what I've done. I've said, so is this correct that what you were saying a moment ago is that information including crimes in villages and towns would be given to the government in written reports. The witness agreed. The government including Stojicic and yourself would then discuss these issues, and then my learned friend jumped up. So I was looking at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we are talking about decision-making, and I think Mr. Weber is right that sometimes and say no decisions were made. So to extrapolate a decision-making process where -- or if you would include that these matters were sometimes or often not decided at all, if I see item 2, no particular decisions were adopted with regard to the report. So that means that is the absence of decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But I am a not suggesting that decisions were always made. I'm saying, is this how decisions were made when they were made. I'm not suggesting -- of course decisions were not always made, but of course there has to be a process by which decisions were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Item 3, conclusion, the Ministry of Justice and Administration shall give its opinion regarding this. What decisions then are you actually referring to as they appear in this document, say look at this, look at that, look at that, and then you can extrapolate from them. No problem with that. Could you point at the decisions you had in your mind. Or is it about the invalids which later appear in the minutes, I don't think that you are focussing on them very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't have a particular decision in mind. I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but if you want to extrapolate something, then at least you have -- there must be a clear basis from where you start extrapolating. Now, if that is about decision-making, that means that we need a couple of decisions in order to start extrapolating or are you, or do you just want to point at the way in which matters were discussed, which is not decision-making but is the way of how the meeting was held. Mr. Weber is right that it should be more transparent in what you are actually using as your basis for, as you said, the extrapolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the basis I was using -- in item 2 information is provided, a discussion is had. In this particular instance it appears a decision was not made. My questions were designed to ask the witness, is this the process by which decisions were made. In this instance no decision was made but that doesn't in any way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, don't you think that that could confuse to say is that the usual way of making decisions then you give an example of where no decisions were made. That might -- is this to say that usually if decisions were needed that no decisions were made. That's also a way of extrapolating. Is that what you -- the extrapolation is -- are you putting to the witness that usually where decisions or where matters were reported that no decisions were made? Is that what you are asking him?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, I was asking him, is this, as reflected in item 2, the way that the government went from information to the point of decisions or non-decisions. Either way. That's the point. The point is made, and it's the same point in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could argue on that. Let's ask then the witness. Mr. Bogunovic, was it usual that once reports were discussed that no decisions were made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were some points on the agenda whereby information was heard but no decisions were made. Sometimes it did happen, a proposal was put forth for the decision to be made by the Assembly, which was authorised to make them. Sometimes the government made decisions on the information we were provided. This is just information. There was information that was discussed, and there was information that was acted upon by way of were making a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So I do understand that if any reports were put on the table, that this resulted in either deciding on the matter or not deciding on the matter, is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There could have been a discussion without any decision or alternatively decisions were made at the end of such discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And sometimes though the matter was not discussed at all, is that also understood well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was always a discussion. However, sometimes information was discussed without any decision. There are also points on the agenda which called for decisions, and we did make them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes even without discussion, is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if you want to explore the matter further, but of course, it's not clear to me what way -- what do we learn from this, the Chamber of course is eager to understand fully what you want to demonstrate by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll try to bring the point some focus. If I -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you've just said two things. You've said there was always discussion and then in response to His Honour Judge Orie, you said you agreed with the honourable judge that sometimes decisions were made without discussion. Was there discussion for decisions made at the government sessions or not?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such things on the agenda where only proposal was given for adoption, and there was no need for a discussion, things were adopted and it all depended on the importance of the matter at hand. In other words, not every decision could be made by the government and likewise, there were some points on the agenda which were proposals for adoption and adoptions were indeed made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you agree that there was always discussion about how to deal with crime in the SBWS region, crime against civilians?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the most sensitive issues that we discussed. We had to discuss it, of course. Usually such discussions involved several ministers, the prime minister. I would say that over half the number of ministers participated in the discussion because it was the most sensitive issue, and it was the matter of life and death for the citizens who resided in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. And these discussions led to decisions by the SBWS government as to how to protect the local civilians, is this correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I believe that -- can we just have it clear, I see the witness is still looking at the document in front of him that says no decisions were adopted. If we could have some distinction between, are we talking about Assembly minutes and making of a decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, of course, the -- outside the whole of the problem. The matter, the fact that no decision was reflected here or even that no decision was made does not finally mean that never a decision was made on the matter and that again, Mr. Jordash, makes it so important to know exactly what is our starting point for extrapolating. If you say is it what we find here does it reflect what happened at those meetings, if it does, then at least on some points no decisions were made. At least not after the matter had been discussed on the basis of those reports. Perhaps elsewhere, other time, other place, I do not know. But let's try to be as factual as possible and not to get confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm having real difficulty understanding how to approach the issue. I'm simply trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps let's be very practical. I may have a solution for you, Mr. Jordash, which is the following: We first take a break and since I cannot continue to hear this case after the break and since my colleagues indicated to me that they thought it would be in the interest of justice to continue, you may have less problems after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Weber still would be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, finally, Mr. Jordash, I'm your problem, not Mr. Weber. We will take a break first, perhaps you'll give it some time to think over, and I might briefly discuss with my colleagues who will take over after the break what was my problem and we'll then see whether they have a similar problem, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break, and we resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us resume the session in French and in the absence of Judge Orie pursuant to Rule 15 bis of the Rules of Procedure. Before we start, there are two aspects we need to deal with. First of all, I would like to remind the Defence that they have another 20 minutes for both Defence counsels as yesterday the court had decided to grant an overall amount of time of three hours for the Defence cross-examination. You've already used up 2 hours and 40 minutes. This may raise a problem unless Mr. Petrovic doesn't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is a problem. It is possible that we misunderstood Your Honours' decision. However, I believe there is a basis to perhaps revisit that decision because I believe my learned friend has put relevant questions only, and I believe my questions will be too. I would kindly ask that you revisit your decision to explore further the option offered by Judge Orie yesterday. He said that if the questions posed are deemed relevant, that the Chamber would reconsider the time-limit. I would kindly ask you to consider that, and at this moment I can tell you that I will need at least an hour and a quarter. I will try to cut it short as much as possible and to focus on the most important things, but I would kindly ask that you revisit your decision particularly in view of the fact that the position yesterday was not perfectly clear in the sense of how much time we might get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jordash, how long will you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Finish in five minutes, Your Honours. May I also endorse Mr. Petrovic's comments and just also highlight that some time was taken up by His Honour Judge Orie's questions and also the lengthy discussion concerning the objection, so I would also throw that into the general balance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Jordash, you will need another three minutes, and Mr. Petrovic, the Court grants you one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jordash, the floor is yours. As regards the controversy before the break, since this is not really clear to the Court, you are entitled to ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, I want to deal with this very quickly. Would you agree that the decisions concerning the setting up of police forces and protecting civilians were exclusively made by the government of the SBWS as opposed to having anything do with Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that the government made such decisions and that we consulted amongst ourselves about the best way to do that. Such decisions were made at the sessions of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Based on local information collected at the behest of the SBWS government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender P -- sorry, may I tender Rule 65 ter 2669, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document is admitted into evidence. Could you give it a reference number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D76.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Quickly ... Your Honours, this was -- the exhibit we've just tendered is an exhibit was P568 marked for identification. I'm getting a nod from the Prosecution too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Apologise, we tendered a group of 12 documents yesterday, this was one of the 12 documents, so I had forgotten also that it received an MFI number at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why was that -- why was it MFI'd? Why could it not be admitted completely? I don't quite remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I believe that there was some guidance on wanting additional information in the form of a bar table as to the relevance of each of the documents in their sections that was provided by the Chamber to the Prosecution yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I suppose it could be admitted without any conditions now. So the document is admitted into evidence completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, I've got to be extremely quick now, so I want to ask you about a comment you made in your second statement P554 where you stated that Stanisic was the link between Milosevic and Arkan and Badza. Do you recall making that comment?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a conversation between Hadzic and me when we discussed Badza and his conduct as well as his work. Goran told me then that the link between Badza and Milosevic was Jovica Stanisic, those were his words, and I can't say anything more than that. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you are not suggesting there was a link between Stanisic and Arkan? You are not suggesting that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection. That was not the question that was originally posed. If counsel would like to put the statement to him and have the witness comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be easier to provide the witness with the exact reference where this comment is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: P554 on the screen, please. At page 4 of the English and page 4 of the -- page 5 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, apologies to the Chamber and my learned friend, but we no longer have e-court on the screen. I don't know whether this is only our problem or does everyone in the courtroom have the same problem?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seem to be problems with e-court and it's not possible to display the documents for the moment. Now, we are talking about the witness statement of February the 8th, 2007, and it's paragraph 18 in English, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of Mr. Petrovic for him to be able to follow the deliberations and for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And before you proceed, D76 has become P568. Exhibit P568. You may ask your question, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, the statement says at paragraph 18: "Slobodan Milosevic controlled Hadzic through Arkan and Badza, and Stanisic was the link between Milosevic and Arkan and Badza." Is it the case that you base that comment on something that Hadzic once told you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I based that on Hadzic's words.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But throughout 1991 and 1992, you personally saw nothing which corroborated that assertion by Hadzic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no occasion to see that myself. I can't say anything other than what he had conveyed to me, Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And from what you said a moment ago, what Hadzic in fact said to you was that Stanisic was the link between Milosevic and Badza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what Hadzic told me, and I shared it with you, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then you assumed -- you made the assumption that that relationship included Arkan; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Arkan is concerned, he could frequently be seen with Badza. Based on that fact that they were together frequently, I made the assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogunovic. I've got nothing further. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I was going to stop you. Mr. Petrovic, you have the floor. Mr. Bogunovic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic as the counsel for Mr. Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement you say that at some point in time you were assigned an office in Sid. Who provided you with that office and when, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got an office towards the end of August. The municipality of Sid secured the premises so that I could locate my headquarters there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement when discussing Sid, you also mentioned a person by the name of Petkovic. As far as I understand, he was a colonel with the JNA. Can you tell us who Colonel Petkovic is and what was his position?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisa Petkovic was a JNA colonel. He had a security function with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In what unit? What establishment?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that off the cuff. I really don't know. I don't think I knew even then, but I did meet with him for a number of consultations or meetings, and he provided a link between Sid and the surrounding villages such as Mirkovci and Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement of 2003 which is P553 in paragraph 17, concerning Sid, it says: "As for Sid, Colonel Petkovic occasionally invited me to discuss things that were to be done." Can you tell me what your relationship between you and Petkovic looked like? You say that he invited you to discuss things. Did he also tell you how to go about things, can you explain your relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he suggested some things to me and at times he also issued orders to me. There were some things we jointly discussed in order to try to find the best possible means to achieve our goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's discuss the category of issues whereupon he issued you with orders. Can you tell me what kind of things did Colonel Petkovic order you to do?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll use an example. He ordered me to go to the village of Lovas to tell the White Eagles to leave it within the next 24 hours. If they refused, I was to tell them that he would be forced to arrest them and disarm them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, did you comply with that order of his?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I got in touch with Mr. Jovic who was their commander at the time and indeed they withdrew from Lovas the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 65 ter number 3910. I can't see it in e-court, but I hope it can be shown to the witness. Your Honour, I don't know whether you will be able to follow unless your e-court is working. Unfortunately I don't have a hard copy. 65 ter 3910.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem being, Mr. Petrovic, is that we can -- we do see the document on our screens, but the public cannot see the documents on e-court, which is a problem in a way. Would you be able to wait a couple of minutes because the technicians will be here in a couple of minutes. Would you be able to perhaps put questions which do not involve the documents, which do not involve e-court documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm concerned with you being able to see the document. As far as I'm concerned, this is a public document, and we can continue. I only want you to be able to see it and perhaps we can broadcast it later for the public. If you can see it, I believe it would be wise to simply continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Weber, what do you think about this since the public will not be able to see the document? What is your opinion on this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If I could just check one thing very quickly. Your Honour, I think for the time being I see that this was part of our first bar table motion filed on the 23rd November, 2009, and there may be some outstanding protective measures with respect to this document, so I think it might be best to not broadcast it at this time anyway and proceed. Sorry, it took me a second to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. This does resolve the problem. In fact, you may continue then, we do have access to the document ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The English booth cannot see the document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, have a look at the document. It comes from the first military district issued by Lieutenant-General Zivo Toponovic [phoen]. Have you been able to see it, to view it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 1, please. It says that units are ordered to establish full control in the area of responsibility of those units. Particular attention needs to be paid to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Petrovic kindly slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrovic, would you please slow down. The interpreters do not have access to the document, so you would have to slow down slightly and read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I'm rushing because of time constraints, but this actually does not work in my favour, I fully understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'll read it out again. Establish full control within the AORs of the units. Particular attention needs to be paid to the functioning of the military authorities in all settlements and any influence on the part of local authorities should be disallowed pending full civilian control of the area. Mr. Bogunovic, the contents of this order, do they reflect your knowledge with regard to the position of army commands vis-a-vis civilian authorities during the relevant period of time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So military authorities dominated in full in all segments important for the carrying out of operations and security in the territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Look at paragraph 2, please. Does it say precisely what Colonel Petkovic ordered you to do?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now look at paragraph 5 in the same document and tell me, do you know if this part of this order has ever been executed, and it refers to the establishment of the military district and military departments in the villages and towns in Western Srem and Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document please be admitted either as a Prosecution document or as a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objections. I believe it's been tendered by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we have a Defence document, and this document will be admitted into evidence. Would you please give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That will be Exhibit D76 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, could you briefly tell us, if you know, of course, what is the area of responsibility of the military unit? What does that term imply?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An area of responsibility is an area where troops are deployed, or rather, an area where troops are present and for which troops are responsible. Anything that happens in such an area has to be reported to the army. The army has to be aware of what is going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, at the relevant time in October 1991, were there any indicia that a paramilitary unit committed crime in the territory of the village of Lovas; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, is it correct that based on such information, the Yugoslav People's Army carried out an investigation about what had happened in the area?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The JNA carried out an investigation. That's why I was issued an order to make all the paramilitary formations leave Lovas within the next 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogunovic. In other words, either you or anybody else were not involved in an investigation. An investigation was carried out but the military investigative organ; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly tell me, please, if you know, do you know in the autumn of 1991, was there still the regional SUP of the autonomous province of Vojvodina in existence, or in other words, was the organisational schematic or the organisation of the SUP kept as it was in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia previously?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That means that the provincial SUP of Vojvodina was autonomous with regard to the organs of the interior or rather with the MUP of the Republic of Serbia in Belgrade, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a few more questions with this regard or with regard to the Yugoslav People's Army. When were the elements of the Zemin Corps transferred to Erdut, Dalj, and the area around there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly. As far as I can remember I believe that that was in late July or early August.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which unit of the JNA were at the time which was the summer or autumn 1991 deployed in the territory of Baranja?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, when was the Guard's Brigade deployed in the southern part of the region, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that happened around the 20th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, do you know what the OG South was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, Mr. Bogunovic, when was the circle closed around the city of Vukovar? In other words, when was it surrounded from the north and from the south? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that happened sometime in the month of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We've been referring to the Guards Brigade here. Could you -- and accompanying units. Could you please tell us something about the strength of those units, what equipment they had, what kind of a military formation it was? Very briefly if you know something or if you saw something?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, I can't tell you much. I was not there when they were deployed, I could not see how big the unit was and what equipment they had at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bogunovic. You were in the southern part of the area. You hail from Negoslavci, your office was in Sid which means that you moved south of the city of Vukovar in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Yugoslav People's Army on the 7th of May, 1991 sent its tank units and took both parts of the 25th of May bridge between Backa Palanka and Ilok?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us according to the best of your recollection, is it correct that the Yugoslav People's Army had their first flights in Croatia in Ilok in [indiscernible] on the 7th of July 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, is it true that towards the end of July 1991, 50 tanks were deployed in the vicinity of Ilok together with some other armoured vehicles of the Yugoslav People's Army and that they were getting closer to Ilok at the beginning of May 1991?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were heavy artillery deployed around Ilok including tanks, but I don't know their numbers. I didn't see how many there were, but I did see some pieces of heavy artillery deployed around Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that on the 26th of September, 1991, the Yugoslav People's Army issued an ultimatum to armed formations in the village of Lovas and two days later in the village of Babska [phoen]. According to that ultimatum they were supposed to surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Yugoslav People's Army at the beginning of October 1991 issued an ultimatum to the armed formations which were deployed in the town of Ilok, it was the same ultimatum according to which they were supposed to surrender and surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at the beginning of October 1991, a commission from the city of Ilok engaged in daily negotiations with the representatives of Novi Sad and Belgrade corps of the JNAs in Backa Palanka and Sid regarding the further destiny of the city of Ilok and its inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the 12th of October a decision was taken by the city Assembly of the city of Ilok to hold a referendum, and at that referendum a decision would be reached as to whether the ultimatum issued by the JNA would be complied with?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the results of the referendum were, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a decision was taken to let the military know that the citizens of Ilok wished to leave Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 14th of October, 1991, in the presence of Dragoljub [indiscernible] a JNA general and the representatives of the European commission an agreement was dictated about the surrender of the town of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after that agreement was reached, several thousand, about 8.000 people, which constituted almost an entire population of Ilok on the 17 of October loaded JNA trucks and set out towards Lipovac and further afield into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that very few people remained living in Ilok after that and I am talking about Croatians, effectively the entire population in October 1991 emigrated and moved into the interior of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that none of the members of the government on which you were minister did not participate in negotiations about the resettlement of the population of Ilok in October of 1991, those negotiations involved only representatives of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were not there. Only the army. Representatives were there negotiated with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, is it true that, as it says in your statement, that all Croats, Slovaks, and others who remained in Croatia after that mass exodus in October remained in their houses until the peaceful integration of Eastern Slavonia in 1997 or 1998?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bogunovic, is it correct that after the fall of Ilok, certain representatives of the -- of your government demanded from the JNA to assume some positions in the judiciary in the police but that demand was never met; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who issued that demand and how did the JNA respond to it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the minister of justice, Vojin Susa, who told them that we already had our own judiciary and the police and that we were in a position to try people in Srem and Baranja. He -- Arkan also attending that meeting and Arkan was of the same opinion. He wanted for all the detained persons to remain in Vukovar and to be put on trial there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bogunovic. In your statement from 2003, which is P554, you say that at the beginning of December 1991, the Red Berets appeared in Ilok. My question to you is this: Is it true that you didn't know anything about who had sent those people and why they had been sent to the town of Ilok?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I did not have any information to that effect, or rather, I did not have any encounters with them. I did not have an opportunity to talk to them about the situation in Ilok, the situation that prevailed in Ilok at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, is it true that those men were billeted in a house in the town of Ilok as well as in the vinery above Ilok and that as far as you know they never moved from there, they never participated in any combat during the relevant time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time combat operations were over, therefore, they could not be engaged. I stated that they were in a house in Ilok known as the white house and they also had some of their members billeted above Ilok in the vinery there, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that combat operations were over at the moment when the Red Berets appeared in the area; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the Red Berets were not involved in the internal relations of the area as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my work is concerned, as far as the work of my colleagues and the civilian authorities in Ilok is concerned, after the departure of the army, they didn't get involved in what we did, in our decision-making processes, they did not have any contacts with us. They were there, but they did not interfere in our business.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bogunovic. Is it true that you never received any information about people being abused or ill-treated by the Red Berets? This is what you stated in 2007; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that there was no ill treatment or --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If -- we are going a little quick. If we could get a paragraph reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. P554, paragraph 8, where Mr. Bogunovic said, "As far as anything else is concerned, I have never received any complaints from civilians about the ill treatment on the part of the Red Berets."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, is it true that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I don't see that in that paragraph. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 8 where it says -- in the middle of that paragraph, paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I see the section where it says, there was a case when a woman refused to hand over -- she came to Crisis Staff to complain, so I see that there's an indication of a complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Mr. Petrovic is referring to the sentence which reads as follows: "I never received information about physical abuse as committed by the Red Berets." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's limited. There were never any complaints of physical abuses, but of course, there were some people complaining about other things. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bogunovic, you yesterday mentioned three or four cases of other complaints concerning vehicles; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Here in your statement it is mentioned that a Croatian lady complained because somebody wanted to take her vehicle. She came to complain. I told her not to give them their vehicle, and she kept the vehicle; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And those are the only examples of complaints about the conduct of those people while they were billeted in the territory of Ilok; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV BOGUNOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. There may have been some other petty things, but there was nothing important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
